title: The Cell Membrane
subject: Biology
text:
Every cell is surrounded by a thin boundary called the cell membrane. It separates the inside of the cell from its surroundings and decides which substances may pass.

The membrane is built from a double layer of phospholipids. Each phospholipid has a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails, so the tails point inwards and the heads face the water on both sides.

Proteins are embedded in this bilayer. Some span the whole membrane and form channels; others sit on one surface and act as receptors that receive signals from other cells.

The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a moving sea of lipids in which proteins drift like icebergs. Cholesterol between the lipids keeps the membrane from becoming too stiff or too fluid.

Small uncharged molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the membrane by simple diffusion. They move from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration without any energy from the cell.

Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane. Water moves towards the side with the higher concentration of dissolved particles.

In a hypotonic solution, water enters an animal cell until it may burst. In a hypertonic solution the cell loses water and shrinks. In an isotonic solution there is no net movement of water.

Ions and larger molecules such as glucose need help from transport proteins. In facilitated diffusion, carrier or channel proteins let them through, still down their concentration gradient and without energy.

Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient. It needs energy in the form of ATP. The sodium-potassium pump, for example, moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions in for each ATP it uses.

Very large particles enter by endocytosis: the membrane folds around the particle and pinches off as a vesicle. Exocytosis is the reverse process, used for example to release hormones.

A common mistake is to think that diffusion stops when the concentrations are equal. In fact the molecules keep moving; only the net movement becomes zero.
